messages.subject: frequentist data-augmentation
parts:
Hi all,

this post is more about a curiosity that I just explored rather than a burning practical question. (I meant to write "a riddle", too, but then while writing I began to understand things and so I believe there is no riddle anymore to me.) Furthermore, it may interest only those of you who know what data-augmentation in BUGS is (in the sense of Royle et al., JCGS, 2007; see also the Royle & Dorazio, 2008, hierarchical modeling bible).

A typical example of data-augmentation (DA) is when you turn a population-size estimation-type of model ('closed captures' in MARK) into a static occupancy model, after adding to the observed detection histories of the n observed animals some arbitrary large enough number of M-n all-zero detection histories. In the resulting model, the occupancy paramater psi takes on the role of the abundance parameter N in the original analysis. The usual population size estimator N_hat is the sum of the estimated latent occurrence states in the occupancy model. DA makes the fitting of many complex hierarchical models much easier in the BUGS world (or more generally, with MCMC), because it fixes the dimension of the parameter space.

I had long been wondering about whether DA couldn't be done with maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) as well and so I tried it out with unmarked (function occu()) for the two models which in the capture-recapture literature are known as models M0 and Mt (having entirely constant and time-dependent detection probability, respectively). I used simulated data with 3 occasions and BUGS code from chapter 6 in our BPA book (code available on request for anybody who's interested). Truth was N=100 for both, and p = 0.4 in the former and p =  (0.214, 0.472, 0.522) in the latter.

I found this: all parameter estimates agree very well for the Bayesian and the frequentist sides of the world, with the exception of the 95% uncertainty intervals for population size (when it is computed as the sum of the occurrence states in BUGS) and computed in unmarked by parametric bootstrapping. (This discrepancy was the reason for why I had originally intended to call this post a riddle report.)

Here is a brief overview of the results:

Here, omega corresponds to the occupancy parameter and p is p. realized.N is the population size estimate obtained
by adding up the latent occurrence indicators (sum(z) in my favourite notation), while expected.N is the population size estimate for a hypothetical
replicate study (which is given by M * omega). The point estimates of the two latter are identical (up to MC error), but the uncertainty in the latter is bigger,
because it contains an additional variance component due to sample-to-sample variation.

MLEs from unmarked (not logit scale for both params)

As for the population size estimate with unmarked (via sum(ranef(fm)@post[,2,])), I get:
110.9506

Bootstrapping (with 1000 sim reps) gives me this 95% interval:
     2.5%     97.5%
 90.49352 135.20914

So, using the bootstrap we estimate the expected population size rather than the realized one. See Effort and Fewster (Oikos 122: 918–928, 2013) for more about this distinction. Arguably, the realized population size is more interesting to ecologists and especially managers.

As for the population size estimate with unmarked (via sum(ranef(fm)@post[,2,])), I get:

Bootstrapping (with 1000 sim reps) gives me this 95% interval:

So what should we learn from this ?
(1) Of course you can do data-augmentation in a non-bayesian way. Perhaps when teaching (or self-teaching) DA this may help to show or know, since it takes away the awe of Bayes from a concept that is already quite challenging to grasp, despite its simplicity.

(2) As is typically the case, bayesian estimates and MLEs agree very well numerically, when vague priors are used (unless sample sizes are very small).

(3) I found interesting the intricacies of the difference between finite-population inference (represented by the realized.N, for my particular population) and population inference (expected.N, for any "comparable" population). With BUGS, it is simple to get either of them, but I don't know how I could get finite-population inference using DA in a frequentist framework.

Happy Tuesday,

Marc

About ~year ago (I believe), Andy Royle and Chris Sutherland co-taught a 'SCR' workshop here at Cornell. A lot of the early part of the material was based on using a DA approach in *BUGS. About the end of the first day, about 4-5 of the attendees who were 'frequenstists' by training came up to me and asked for a 'simple explanation' of DA. The obvious 'bridge' (to me) was using DA, and occupancy, to estimate abundance. I've attached the result. It is part of a larger 'occupancy' chapter in the MARK book -- and has benefited from comments from Larissa Bailey and Darryl MacKenzie. It covers the 'finitie poipulation' inference question. 

As Marc notes, the larger 'riddle' (his words) is how to handle the estimate of uncertainty for abundance. I have more to say on this (based on comments from Darryl, and more recently, Andy Royle), but wanted to pass this along.

messages.author: 0227543d81e2924c
messages.subject: Re: frequentist data-augmentation
parts:
About a year ago, Chris Sutherland and Andy Royle gave an SCR workshop here at Cornell -- much of the early part of the presentation made 'use' of DA in various contexts -- including abundance estimation. At the end of day one, I had 3-4 people with 'frequentist' training, who knew me in the context of 'MARK' and 'the MARK book' come up and ask for a simple explanation of DA, and why it worked. So, I cobbled together an 'explanation by example' -- using DA in an occupancy context in MARK to estimate abundance. It is part of a 'too-be'published soon' chapter on using MARK for occupancy analysis. It covers the basic ideas, and the estimation of abundance using occupancy, based on DA. It deals with the finite population sample issue Marc mentions. The text is still 'draft', but has already benefited from comments from Larissa Bailey, Darryl MacKenzie, and more recently Andy Royle. 

The technical 'riddle' that needs more work is the estimation of uncertainty for abundance. In the attached, there is an approach based on ideas that Darryl came up with, which Andy has suggested is 'quite sensible', but there is more to be done here. I'll add some further thoughts when I get into the office.
